en: Preface to the Commentary on the Song of Realizing the Way by Master Miaokong Fohai of Lingyan, Suzhou:

I have often observed that within our own tradition, those who fish and hunt through texts and language are extremely numerous; yet, those who shine forth through the ages and whose words remain as savory as minced meat in the mouths of the people are few.
As for Yongjia’s composition of a song to realize the Way, it is concise, consisting of no more than two thousand characters. In the past...

Even a lowly milkmaid tending the hearth can strive to look up to and aspire toward this Way, vying with one another to recite his bequeathed verses and fragments; how much more so for scholars and monastics?

Like ants swarming toward a cloud-borne chariot, they need not wait for further instruction. Viewed from this perspective, there are none who have not planted the roots of virtue in past lives, such that their practice and realization correspond.
Though they borrow the samādhi of the tongue to sport within the human world, they have already liberated themselves.
To practice toward the Buddhas and Patriarchs, scholars exhaustively investigate their source; this is much like holding a conch shell to measure the ocean or grasping a tube to peer at the heavens.
Truly, it is no exaggeration that the Western Land calls this the *Sūtra on Realizing the Way*. Whenever I reflect upon this episode of the Buddha’s deeds, it remains fixed between my teeth and jaws;
even in the midst of the most hurried moments, I have been unable to forget it. O assembly of talented ones, you who are but withered Zen practitioners...
[The Master] replied: "Externally, I am but a man of meager learning who has heard little; I merely drew my robe to ask questions, and thus this matter eventually reached us.

Who would have expected that my junior disciple Dezui, having followed me for so long, would advance day by day and month by month until compiling these into a collection? One day he presented it to me, seeking a preface so that it might be transmitted to future generations.
I was struck with astonishment. After a long while, I questioned him, saying: 'The entire Tripiṭaka and even half of it are all considered essential.'"
The character "foot" (腳) is composed of eight strokes; when inverted, it becomes "Miao" (邈). Bodhidharma faced the wall in silence; the Tathāgata had no dharma to preach.
In the past, Yongjia was already carving a wound upon his own flesh—how could one further apply needles and mustard seeds to that scar?
You, sir, are merely peddling entangling vines; will you not bring trouble upon me? He replied: "I deeply lament that the Buddha-Dharma is as precarious as a stack of bricks."

Eggs [of the Dharma]: the predecessors have passed away, and the younger generation lacks renown. I feel ashamed that I have failed to repay the diligent efforts of those who personally instructed and guided me by the ear.

As you, Master, have said, these matters can only be understood by those of great capacity and superior wisdom—those who attain awakening upon hearing once and proceed without waiting for the shadow of a whip.

However, for those of dull faculties and late learners, one must certainly rely on the trap and the snare [as expedient means]. Since you, Master, have spoken no words, what can this humble disciple describe? Thus...
This was a series of evasions; it was like attempting to add feet to a snake or attach wings to a tiger. I had merely shown him this secondary teaching.

At that moment, there happened to be a Magistrate named Mei present, who had settled his spirit within the inner scriptures and held them ever in mind. Upon seeing these writings, he was moved to realization and wept aloud.
He then offered a gold-threaded wooden plaque, hoping that in the future they might walk hand-in-hand together through the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
This is indeed a most excellent assembly; how could it be anything less than a great benefit?
Therefore, I have composed this preface with a brush. Written at the time of the Shaoxing Bingyin year while residing at Lingyan, by the old man Qu Yi, Zhi’ne.
Preface to the *Song of Realizing the Way* annotated by Master Miaokong of Lingyan.

The attendant Dezui recounted that in the past, at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the World-Honored One held up a single flower. Kāśyapa smiled, and [the Buddha] continued, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye;
I entrust it to you. This is called "realization. Furthermore, Master Yongjia originally practiced the *Tiantai* method of *śamatha*.

While practicing contemplation within the four modes of deportment, he constantly merged with meditative observation. Consequently, he went to Caoxi to consult the Sixth Patriarch; through their exchange of questions and answers, he received the Patriarch’s seal of approval.
The Patriarch invited him to stay for one night, and because of this, he was known as "One-Night Awakening" (Yixiu Jue).
He then composed this song, recording in writing the Way he had realized; therefore, it is called the *Song of Realizing the Way*.
Annotated by Venerable Lingyan Miaokong;
prepared for publication through the sponsorship of the disciple in study Mei Ruren, who provided the funds and commissioned the craftsmen to carve the woodblocks.
Regarding the "Single-Syllable Dharma-Gate" (*ekākṣara-dharmamukha*): according to my own examination of the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra*, it states that there is not a single dharma among all dharmas;
this is called the Single-Syllable Dharma-Gate. See Volume 2, page 23 of the *Zongjing Lu*.
"Not seeing. This means transcending sound and surpassing form, departing from seeing and severing hearing. As it is said: "At the moment of seeing-seeing, seeing is not seeing;
even seeing is already apart from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it. Now tell me: when you do not see, what exactly is it that you do not see?

The man of the Way who has severed learning and is non-active does not learn of either existence or non-existence; reaching the state of no-learning is called "severing learning. He acts all day long, yet never acts.
This is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, to transcend the dust of the emotions is what is called being a "leisurely Way-person.
One does not eliminate deluded thoughts nor seek the truth;
for delusion is fundamentally the Way and cannot be said to be eliminated, while the true nature is fundamentally empty—how could one seek it further? Nevertheless, as it is said:
This is so. One must advance one more step to reach the state where there is neither seeking nor removal.
The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature;
truth and delusion share the same source, and principle and phenomena are non-dual. The very nature of ignorance is Buddha-nature; it need not be abandoned.

It is delusory to seek buddha-nature separately. If one is apart from delusion, there is no buddha-nature. Yet, buddha-nature is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it both existent and non-existent.
If one says that buddha-nature can be immediately realized, how does this differ from adding more mud to the top of the earth?
The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.
Having realized that clarity is precisely the Buddha-nature, the body follows the transformation of wisdom, and one also thoroughly understands the illusory form-body manifest before one.
This is precisely the Dharma-body of true emptiness. Yet, it was said above: "Do not eliminate delusion, nor seek the truth; neither truth nor delusion is established. It was further said:
"The actual nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body. This is because true emptiness is profoundly still.
Although it cannot be sought, it is eternally perfect; although it manifests before one, it is utterly ungraspable.
"It can be sought. The Dharmakāya is fully awakened and realized; there is not a single thing. The original source, one's own fundamental nature, is the true Buddha.

The Master feared that people might still think it possible to intellectually grasp the Dharmakāya, and therefore he reiterated: "The Dharmakāya is fully awakened and realized; there is not a single thing."
Furthermore, it is said: "To have not a single thing" does not mean to remove things; rather, it means that within each and every thing, its very substance is emptiness.
Thus, when there is not a single thing, then everywhere is the Real, and nothing is not the Way. Therefore, it is said: "The fundamental source and original nature is the Heaven-born Buddha."
The five aggregates are like floating clouds, empty in their coming and going; the three poisons are like bubbles on water, empty in their appearing and disappearing.
The five aggregates are unreal, comparable to floating clouds; though they come and go within the great void, the nature of that great void remains unchanged.
Fundamentally, there is neither movement nor stillness; the three poisons are not solid, being as upright as empty bubbles.

Although they emerge and submerge within the great ocean, the waters of the great ocean never arise or cease. Thus one knows that illusory and false forms and appearances inherently possess arising and ceasing, whereas the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is primordial and fundamentally free from change.
Realizing the true mark (lakṣaṇa) wherein neither person nor phenomena exist, one extinguishes the karma of Avīci hell in a single instant.
In the principle and phenomena of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), not a single speck of dust is received. Since both person and phenomena are non-existent, who is there to receive the karma?
If one deceives sentient beings with false speech, one will bring upon oneself the punishment of having one's tongue plucked out for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Fearing that future generations might find it difficult to believe,
the Master made a great vow and suddenly awakened to the Tathāgata-dhyāna.
Without passing through successive stages, one transcends directly; therefore, it is called "sudden awakening. It is perfectly integrated and complete, lacking nothing and having no excess;
this is called "Tathāgata-dhyāna."
The essence of the myriad practices of the six pāramitās is perfect and complete.
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom are called the six pāramitās; taken together, they constitute the six pāramitās.
The myriad practices are extensive, yet their essence is but the one mind. Therefore it is said: "In its substance, it is perfectly round;
within the dream, the six realms are clearly present; upon awakening, all is empty, with not even a great chiliocosm remaining."
Within a dream, myriad things are in turmoil; upon awakening, they are suddenly gone, not one remaining. The six realms and the great trichiliocosm are all transformations of the deluded mind.
Since the deluded mind is itself illusory, all worldly phenomena lack any substantial reality.
There is neither sin nor merit, neither loss nor gain. Within the nature of quiescent extinction, do not seek or inquire.
Since sin and merit are fundamentally empty, they are said to be "non-existent. This is because the body is like an illusion or a dream; how could sin and merit affect it?
If it were like space, how could one seek or inquire after it?
Hitherto, the dusty mirror has never been polished; today it must be clearly scrutinized and broken open.
Sentient beings do not understand the ground of mind, which is like dust upon a mirror. One should seek an enlightened teacher to polish its luster and scour away its impurities.
Who is without thought? Who is without birth? If in truth there is neither birth nor non-birth, call forth the mechanical wooden man and ask him:
"Seeking the Buddha through the application of effort—when will it be accomplished?"
The Master feared that future generations might fail to awaken and fall into the view of annihilationism; therefore, he posed the question:
"Who is it that has no birth? He meant that if one truly realizes no-birth, then such a person is like a wooden man who certainly cannot understand speech.
It is clear that those who cling to no-birth will inevitably fall into nihilism and will not achieve Buddhahood.
Release the four great elements and do not grasp at them; within the nature of quiescent extinction, follow the natural course of drinking and eating.
Since one no longer clings to non-arising, one knows that the four great elements are fundamentally empty. Thus, one dwells in carefree liberation, which is the nature of quiescent extinction.
Pure and fundamental from the beginning, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm. All day long, whether putting on clothes or eating meals, one is entirely within it;
what thing, then, could constrain you?
That all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and all is empty is itself the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment.
The four great elements do not exist; what practices could one perform? Even if there were something to be done, its nature is fundamentally empty and quiescent.
To practice in this manner—how is it any different from the Tathāgata?
He definitively expounds the manifestation of the true Sangha. There are those who, following their own whims, refuse to accept his realization;
yet because the Master’s attainment is authentic, all that he speaks is definitive discourse. "Manifesting the true Sangha" means he is fit to serve as the banner of the Sangha.
However, those of inferior faculties and the Hīnayāna, upon hearing the Mahāyāna taught, are unwilling to accept it.
If you accept this with faith yet still raise frivolous objections, what can I say?
To cut straight to the root is the seal of the Buddhas; to pluck leaves and seek branches is not for me.
"To directly realize the mind and see one's nature to become a Buddha—this is what the successive patriarchs of antiquity have transmitted to one another through their mutual seal of approval.
As for exhausting the scriptures through discussion, picking at leaves and seeking out branches, that is not something I can do."
People do not recognize the maṇi jewel; yet it is personally obtained within the Tathāgatagarbha.
In Sanskrit, *maṇi* means "stainless light," which is a metaphor for the nature of the one true reality.
The nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is precisely the eighth consciousness, the *ālayavijñāna*. This containing consciousness is capable of producing all seeds of both good and evil. To awaken to it—
To realize this is to be a sage; to be deluded by it is to be an ordinary person. Yet all sentient beings possess this single jewel.
It simply fails to manifest because, from beginningless kalpas, the causes and conditions have become deeply entangled.

Thus, while the Tathāgata—by means of the wisdom of the emptiness of nature—encompasses the ten directions and pervades the realm of empty space, this jewel remains brilliantly clear, like a pure lapis lazuli gem containing a precious moon within.
Nevertheless, every person in the world possesses a single pearl. Ask people: "Where is it right now?
Six kinds of divine functions—empty or not empty? A single round radiance—form or formless?
Originally there was one refined spirit, which divided into six harmonious combinations. In the eye it is called seeing; in the ear it is called hearing;
in the hand it is grasping; in the foot it is running. To realize this is the functioning of the spirit; to be deluded by it is to become the six thieves.
Therefore, those who have attained the Way constantly realize emptiness and stillness at the gates of the six sense-faculties. They arise in their very place and cease in every circumstance;
yet the fundamental essence is a perfect radiance, numinous, luminous, and all-pervading, which cannot be displayed.
Indeed, it cannot be sought through sound or form, nor can it be realized through existence or non-existence. Hence it is said: "Emptiness is not empty; form is not form."
By purifying the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), one attains the five powers (*pañcabala*). Only through direct realization can this be known; it is difficult to fathom.

The physical eye, the divine eye, the wisdom-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Buddha-eye are called the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*). Faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are called the five powers.
To purify these five eyes and attain these five powers is the realm of the Great [Awakening]; therefore, one must personally realize and personally awaken to it.
Only then can one truly know; how could one possibly venture to make arbitrary conjectures within it?
It is not difficult to see one's own form when looking in a mirror, but who can ever grasp the moon when trying to catch it in water?
If one attempts to fathom the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment with the limited faculties and vehicles of the Lesser Way, it is like looking at a reflection in a mirror;

it is not that there is nothing to see, but rather that what is seen is not ultimately real. It is also like a troop of monkeys who, seeing the moon in the water, try to grasp it, yet in the end achieve no actual result.
Always walking alone, always treading alone; those who have attained realization travel together upon the path to Nirvāṇa.
This path to Nirvāṇa is the path of neither arising nor ceasing; it is called "the one path," and I have now attained it.

Walking alone and striding forth, he stands loftily above the world; only those who have attained realization share his path, for how could those of inferior faculties and the Lesser Vehicle travel therein with a mind of mere conjecture?
His diction is archaic and his spirit is pure; his manner is lofty by nature. His appearance is haggard and his bones are rigid, so that people do not look upon him with favor.
It is simply because he is so exalted that it is difficult for people to gaze up at him.
This impoverished monk claims to be poor in speech, yet in truth he is poor in body but not poor in the Way.
Can he be called "poor"?
As for poverty, his body is constantly clad in coarse hempen garments; yet as for the Way, his mind harbors a priceless treasure.
Though external conditions may be lacking, his inner path is truly wealthy. Who could possibly afford its price?
Priceless and precious, its utility is inexhaustible; benefiting all things in response to conditions, it never begrudges them.
Manifesting face-to-face, how could there ever be concealment? Its application is endless—what dharma could possibly exist [to limit it]?
The three bodies and four wisdoms are perfectly complete within the essence; the eight liberations and six supernormal powers are the seal of the mind-ground.
These three bodies, four wisdoms, eight liberations, and six supernormal powers are all realized by the Tathāgata without the use of the mind. O practitioners of the profound mystery!
If one can be free from discursive thought, one is identical to the Tathāgata.
The superior person, having made a single resolution, understands everything; the mediocre and inferior persons, despite their extensive learning, have little faith.

When the superior person hears the Way, they practice it with diligence; when the mediocre person hears the Way, they are as if it exists and as if it does not; when the inferior person hears [the Way]...
Dao laughed heartily, clapping his hands.
"I simply take off my coarse clothes from within myself; who can boast of diligence toward the outside?
I merely extinguish the dust of emotions within myself; why rely on boasting of diligence toward the outside?"
Let others slander; let others be wrong. To carry fire to burn the heavens is but to exhaust oneself in vain.
The fire of the Way does not burn the mouth; the water of the Way has not a single drop. Where, then, can slander find its place?
Hearing this, it was as if I were drinking nectar; it dissolved away and entered me all at once into the inconceivable.
Whether coarse words or subtle speech, they all return to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
I contemplate offensive words as being merit; thus, they become my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Transforming evil into good, understanding opposition as compliance: contemplating these harsh words as true spiritual friends, one gives rise to neither enmity nor affection due to slander.
How else could this manifest the power of non-arising compassion and patience?
To be unmoved by praise or blame is the practice of the Tathāgata.
There is the penetration of the ultimate principle (*zongtong*) and the penetration of the verbal teaching (*shetong*).

When the ultimate principle is penetrated but the verbal teaching is not, it is like the sun within the clouds. When the verbal teaching is penetrated but the ultimate principle is not, it is like a snake entering a bamboo stalk.
The tube:
when concentration and wisdom are perfectly luminous, one does not stagnate in emptiness.
When concentration and wisdom are perfectly complete, phenomena and principle are perfectly harmonized; thus, one does not fall into nihilistic emptiness. This is called "not stagnating."
It is not that I alone have now attained realization; the essence of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is identical.
There has never been any discrepancy between the Buddhas of the sands of the Ganges, the patriarchs of successive generations, and what I have realized here and now.
The lion’s roar is spoken with fearlessness; when the hundred beasts hear it, their brains are all split open.
One who is proficient in both the essence and the exegesis, and who is sustained by both meditative concentration and wisdom, is like the lion king, entering and emerging without fear.
Those whose understanding and practice are one-sided and whose views are unclear are like the various small beasts; when they hear the lion’s roar, they do not merely submit, but flee far away.
Their brains were split and their hearts shattered;
the fragrant elephants bolted about, losing their majesty, while the devas and nāgas listened in silence, filled with joy.
"Fragrant elephant" is a metaphor for those of the Lesser Vehicle who possess intellectual understanding but have not yet been able to enter this Mahāyāna. Upon first hearing it...

This is the true teaching. [Ordinary beings] are terrified and frantic, just like a fragrant elephant that, despite its great power, turns back and flees at the mere sound of a lion, not knowing what to do.
As for devas and nāgas, they represent those Mahāyāna bodhisattvas who, upon hearing this true teaching, listen with serene joy, their bodies and minds abiding in peace and happiness.
Wandering through rivers and seas, traversing mountains and hills, he sought teachers and inquired after the Way in order to practice Zen.
This is the Master’s own account of his intent in seeking out instruction.
"Since I recognized the path of Caoxi, I have understood that birth and death are no longer relevant."
The Master received the seal of approval from Caoxi; at the very threshold of birth and death, he was entirely without obstruction.
Walking is Chan, sitting is Chan; whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, his essence remains serene.
Since there is neither birth nor death, movement and stillness are one and the same; meeting the source at every turn, there is nothing that does not hit the mark.
Even when encountering a sharp blade, one remains ever serene; even if encountering lethal poison, one remains ever at ease.
The four great elements are fundamentally empty; the five aggregates are not the self. What cause for fear or resentment could there be in poison, drugs, or sharp blades?
My Master beheld the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and, through many kalpas, was once the Immortal of Forbearance.
This refers to Śākyamuni. In the past, when he was the Rishi Kṣāntivādin, he was harmed by King Kali, yet he never showed a trace of resentment.
This was because he had already realized there is no person and no self; therefore, Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon him a prediction of enlightenment.
This is intended to clarify that what the Teacher has realized is likewise so.
"Time and again born, time and again dead"—these were the words of the Master’s own lament upon his awakening.
From the past until the realization of Nirvana, he had lived and died in vain, unaware of how many kalpas had passed; birth and death drifted on endlessly, without any fixed end.
Since attaining sudden enlightenment and entering the state of non-arising, what cause for sorrow or joy could there be amidst all honors and insults?
With the internal masteries no longer swayed by external objects,
he entered the deep mountains to dwell in an araṇya.
In Sanskrit, this is called *araṇya*; here it is translated as "a place free from strife.
Amidst steep peaks and deep seclusion beneath tall pines, the wild monk sits at ease and in stillness. Dwelling in quietude and solitude, he is truly serene and refined.
White clouds serve as a canopy; flowing waters act as a lute. Carefree and transcending the mundane, lofty and rising above the worldly.
Upon awakening, one realizes that no effort need be exerted; all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are not like this.
All that is created and conditioned runs outward; the merit of non-action does not reside in giving.
Giving while dwelling on signs produces the blessings of rebirth in heaven, yet it is like an arrow shot upward into the void: when its momentum is exhausted, the arrow falls back down.
This will bring about undesirable results in the future.

To practice giving with the expectation of a reward is called "dwelling in signs. Although one may obtain the retribution of rebirth in heaven, one cannot avoid eventual downfall. It is like shooting an arrow into the air;
it merely exhausts oneself in vain.
How can this compare to the gate of the unconditioned true mark? It transcends all at once, entering directly into the stage of the Tathāgata.
In the gate of the true mark, one does not rely on effortful practice; with a single thought of turning the light back upon itself, one reaches the stage of the Tathāgata.
Simply attain the root and do not worry about the branches. It is like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon.
When the root is established, the Way arises. The root is the mind. When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.
Like pure lapis lazuli containing a precious moon, it is translucent both inside and out, shining through and illuminating the ten directions.
How could there then be any stagnation regarding phenomena?
I now untie the wish-fulfilling jewel; benefiting self and others, it is never exhausted.
One who seeks to save others before having saved oneself is the bodhisattva’s resolve; once one’s own awakening is perfected, one is able to awaken others.
When a Tathāgata appears in the world, this wish-fulfilling jewel is precisely this *maṇi* jewel.
It is obtained solely within the *tathāgatagarbha*. Now that I have obtained it, I am equal to the Tathāgata; therefore, my benefit for self and others can never be exhausted.
Today, having realized this single jewel, I bestow it upon the great assembly. Do you see it?
The river moon shines; the pine wind blows. Throughout the eternal night and the clear evening, what is there to do?
Do not form conceptual attachments, for this is the true realm.
The Buddha-nature is the jewel of the precepts, the seal upon the ground of the mind; mist, dew, clouds, and mists are the robes upon its body.
Some call it Buddha-nature; some call it the pearl of precepts. In reality, they are all but the one mind. Therefore, it is called the Seal of the Mind-ground.
When this Seal of the Mind is free from stagnation, the body pervades the ten directions. Thus we know that mists, dew, clouds, and rosy vapors are all but garments upon its substance.
The dragon-subduing alms bowl; the tiger-unlocking staff. Two-pronged golden rings ring out clearly. This is not a matter of displaying form or holding onto empty things;
it is the actual trace of the Tathāgata’s precious staff.
These are the alms bowl and the mendicant’s staff. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued a fire-dragon and a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) with his golden staff;
Master Chou resolved a tiger fight with his staff. These names were established based on specific events. Both of these items are implements for the Tathāgata’s propagation of the Dharma.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, he left them hanging upon a tree; this was surely intended as a legacy for future generations—how could it be in vain?
They merely mark out forms and superficially engage in ritual recitation;
they do not seek the Truth, nor do they sever delusion. They understand that these two dharmas are empty and signless (*animitta*); yet, being signless, they are neither empty nor non-empty.
This is precisely the true mark of the Tathāgata.
Where truth and delusion do not stand, there is clear non-characteristic (*animitta*). Since non-characteristic implies the persistence of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one must also be without emptiness.
If there is no emptiness, then there is nothing that is not empty; this is the true mark of the Tathāgata, like a diamond (*vajra*).
The Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata has said that all marks are no-marks; this is called the true mark.
The mirror of the mind is bright and reflective, free from obstruction; vast and translucent, it pervades the realms of sand. Within its reflection, the myriad phenomena appear in dense array;
this single sphere of light is neither internal nor external.
The mirror of the mind is bright and pure, penetrating clearly through the ten directions; how could the myriad phenomena fail to cast their reflections therein?
To recklessly embrace emptiness and dismiss cause and effect is to invite calamity and transgression amidst a vast and boundless void.
To sink into emptiness and stagnate in quiescence; to deny cause and effect; to fail to understand the emptiness of phenomena while claiming to have realized awakening;

to constantly speak of emptiness with one's mouth while being attached to a dull,顽 (wán) emptiness—such a person is no different from the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). This is the case for those who study the profound mystery (xuán).
One should skillfully employ the mind.
Abandoning existence for the sickness of clinging to emptiness is likewise; it is like avoiding drowning only to throw oneself into fire.
To abandon existence and to cling to emptiness—both are grave illnesses.
Abandon the deluded mind and grasp the True Principle. Yet, the very mind that grasps and abandons becomes artful and hypocritical.
When truth and delusion are equalized, grasping and abandoning become one and the same. As soon as a doubting mind arises, it immediately becomes artful hypocrisy.
Therefore, an ancient worthy said: "Cut off both ends of the road; return home and sit in peace."
When practitioners do not understand this, they engage in cultivation; this truly amounts to mistaking a thief for one's own son.
Beginners who have recently entered the path do not understand the nature of existence and non-existence;
though they practice with diligent hardship seeking to escape the three realms, it is just like mistaking a thief for a son—stealing from their own house while failing to achieve true accomplishment.
The depletion of the Dharma-treasure and the extinction of merit are both caused by nothing other than this mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manas-vijñāna*).
A person who lacks the Way must achieve the non-arising of the single mind; only when the mind is like a blank wall can one enter the Way.
This is truly because when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.

Therefore, through the Chan gate, one brings the mind to its ultimate end; by the power of sudden insight into non-arising, one directly clarifies the mind and realizes Buddhahood by seeing one's nature.
A great man wields the sword of wisdom; the blade of Prajñā is like a diamond flame.
Great Master Zhang was a man of courageous spirit. He should have wielded the sword of wisdom to tear asunder the net of afflictions;
"the edge of Prajñā" describes its sharpness, while "Vajra-flame" takes its strength from its hardness.
Not only can it crush the minds of non-Buddhists; it has long since caused the courage of the heavenly Māras to fail.
These non-Buddhists and heavenly Māras, though clever, lack true wisdom; upon hearing this Perfect Teaching, their hearts are shattered and their spirits collapse.
He thunders the Dharma-thunder and beats the Dharma-drum; he spreads the clouds of compassion and sprinkles the nectar of immortality.

With a single stroke of the Perfect Teaching, all are universally benefited. Like thunder that awakens the hibernating creatures, he rouses them from their slumber; like clouds that provide universal cover, he pities those who are deluded.
Like rain that nourishes all universally—how vast is its benefit!
As dragons and elephants trample through it, the moisture is boundless; those of the three vehicles and five natures are all awakened.
"Dragons and elephants" refers to those of the Supreme Vehicle; upon hearing this thunder of the Dharma and being moistened by this rain, they are extensively and deeply nurtured.
Although those of the three vehicles and five natures have not yet fully attained the supreme benefit, they nonetheless possess a clear awakening.
"The snow mountains are rich and pure, with no admixture; from them flows pure ghee, which I constantly receive."
On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called "Patience. It is said to be rich and succulent; if an ox eats it, it produces nothing but the finest clarified butter (*sarpis*).
This is a metaphor for the unadulterated nature of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*).
The single nature is perfectly interfused with all natures; the single dharma universally contains all dharmas.
To cite the single nature is to encompass all natures; to cite the single dharma is to unify all dharmas. [Repeated phrase omitted].
Yet it has never been small; it is present in all things, yet it has never been many, because there is no dharma that exceeds it.
The single moon universally appears in all waters, and all the moons in the waters are subsumed within that one moon.
The single month is a metaphor for the one mind. All waters are a metaphor for the various worlds.
Only the mind can manifest in all places, yet it is ultimately subsumed within the one mind.
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas enters my own nature; my nature, in turn, merges with that of the Tathāgata.

Ordinary beings and sages are not two; living beings and Buddhas are no different. It is solely because my true nature is identical to that of the Tathāgata that the Dharma-body is able to enter within my nature.
The first stage is fully endowed with all stages. It is neither form nor mind, neither karma nor practice;
it is the perfect ultimate stage that fully encompasses all stages. It cannot be attained by ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles through the means of form, mind, karma, or practice.
In a single snap of the fingers, the eighty thousand gateways are perfectly accomplished; in an instant, the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas are extinguished.
The eighty thousand Dharma gates can be realized in a mere finger-snap; the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas can be brought to an end in a single moment.
All numerical phrases and non-numerical phrases—what connection do they have with my numinous awareness?

"Number" refers to the numerical categories of phenomena, and "phrases" refer to verbal teachings. This nature of numinous awareness cannot be measured by the verbal teachings of phenomenal characteristics, nor can it be attained through the verbal teachings of non-phenomenal characteristics.
It cannot be disparaged; it cannot be praised. Its essence is like empty space, without boundaries or shores.
Space has no marks; what use is there for disparagement or praise?
Without leaving its present location, it is eternally serene. Seek it, and you will find that it cannot be seen.
"Brilliantly manifest within the space between mind and eye, yet its form cannot be seen. Radiantly shining amidst the realm of sensory objects, yet its principle cannot be divided.
Now tell me: where does it reside right now? After a long silence, the Master said, "It turns out it has always been right here."
It cannot be grasped; it cannot be relinquished. Within that which is unobtainable, one simply attains it as such.
The Way has neither "this" nor "that"; it is people themselves who grasp and relinquish. Simply by being free from discrimination, one is the Buddha of Suchness.
Speaking in silence; silent while speaking.
In silence, his voice is like thunder; in speaking, he has neither mouth nor tongue.
The great gate of giving is opened wide, without obstruction.
Unfurling the eight characters, we meet at the entrance.
If someone asks me which school I understand, I reply: "The power of *Mahāprajñā*. *Mahā* is a Sanskrit term;
here it means "great," "much," or "supreme. *Prajñā* means "wisdom. My school takes the absence of... [as its principle].
The *Prajñāpāramitā* is its primary tenet. As for its "power," it is because it can shatter all afflictions (*kleśa*).
Whether [an action] is right or wrong, people do not recognize it; whether one acts in opposition to or in accordance with worldly norms, even the heavens cannot fathom it.
For one who has attained the Way, every transverse and vertical wondrous application is nothing other than the work of a Buddha. Even Heaven cannot fathom such a person;
how much less can ordinary men? Nevertheless, even so, one must truly reach this stage before it can be realized.
"I have already practiced through many kalpas in the past; this is not a matter of idle deception.
Yet these matters are truly no small cause. That I have now attained them could not have been accomplished through practice and realization in a single lifetime or a single kalpa.
It was surely through diligent toil over many kalpas—how could it be a matter of idle deception? The Master feared that later..."
Because their faith and roots were shallow and inferior, they spoke these words.
To raise the banner of the Dharma and establish the fundamental tenets—clearly manifesting the Buddha’s command—it is Caoxi (Huineng) who is so.
Since Bodhidharma came from the West, the transmission has been passed down to the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi. Bodhidharma said: "I have come here for this very purpose."
The Patriarch transmitted the Dharma to save those lost in delusion. "One flower opens into five petals; the fruition is naturally accomplished.

This school of mine transmits mind by means of mind; it does not establish written words. This separate transmission outside the teachings was established as its fundamental principle; truly, this was no small matter.
Had it not been for receiving the Buddha’s prediction and entrustment, how could it have been so?
The first, Kāśyapa, was the foremost transmitter of the lamp. The record of the twenty-eight generations in the Western Heaven is as follows:
At the assembly on Vulture Peak, the Buddha entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to Kāśyapa; Kāśyapa transmitted it to Ānanda.
Thus, through successive patriarchs, it was passed down until the twenty-eighth patriarch, Bodhidharma. This is the record of the Western Heaven.
Having traversed the rivers and seas, he entered this land. In the Western Heaven, Bodhidharma was the first patriarch;
in this land, Bodhidharma is likewise the first patriarch. In the Western Heaven, Kāśyapa was the first patriarch; in this land, it is Bodhidharma who is the first patriarch.
"The transmission of the robe through six generations was renowned throughout the world. As for those who attained the Way thereafter, their number is beyond reckoning.
When Bodhidharma first arrived in this land, the sentient beings here were still shallow in their roots of faith; therefore, he used the robe as a token of faith.
Upon reaching the Sixth Patriarch, however, he observed that the faculties and capacities of sentient beings had already matured, so he ceased the transmission of the robe. He did, however—"
It was transmitted solely through the seal of the mind. Since that time, those who have attained the Way have been as numerous as the vast waters; how could they be counted?
True reality does not stand, and delusion is fundamentally empty. Both existence and non-existence are cast aside, yet it is not an emptiness of emptiness.
Reality and falsehood, existence and non-existence, are all phenomena that exist in mutual opposition. If reality were not established, by what means could falsehood arise?
Once both existence and non-existence have been discarded, even the emptiness that discards them is itself discarded; therefore, it is called "not empty of emptiness."
The twenty gates of emptiness originally have no attachment; the single nature of the Tathāgata’s essence is inherently identical.
The twenty emptinesses originally derive from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. Emptiness is but one; however, in order to dismantle twenty kinds of existence, twenty emptinesses are established.
These emptinesses are themselves empty; when essence and appearance are both fused, this is identical to the essence of the Tathāgata.
Their nature is the same. The mind is the faculty; phenomena are the objects. These two are like stains upon a mirror.
Mind and phenomena, faculties and objects, all arise through mutual dependence; they have never been the true nature. Within the true nature, [they do not exist].
There are these two kinds [of obstructions], like dust and grime upon a mirror.
Only when the stains and blemishes are entirely removed does the light begin to manifest. When both mind and phenomena are extinguished, the nature is truly real.
When the stains are completely purified, the mirror’s light is unimpeded; when mind and phenomena have vanished, the true nature is vast and open. This...
The principle of nature is clear.
Alas for this degenerate dharma and evil age! Sentient beings have meager merit and are difficult to discipline.
Having entered the age of the final dharma, many people are negligent and lax.
The Sage has long since departed, and false views have grown deep; the Māras are powerful while the Dharma is weak, resulting in much resentment and harm.
Since the Sage’s departure is remote, false views have become increasingly profound. Upon hearing this Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), many give rise to hatred and malice.
Even Bodhidharma suffered the striking of his teeth—how much more so in the present age?
Upon hearing the teachings of the Tathāgata’s sudden (sudden) teaching, they regret that it has not been extinguished and destroyed so as to shatter it like a tile.
Abandoning the root to pursue the branches, they cling to phenomenal characteristics; upon hearing the teaching of the sudden Dharma, they immediately seek to extinguish and destroy it.
The deed is formed in the mind; the calamity falls upon the body. There is no need to harbor resentment or complaints, nor to blame others.
It is because the mind has destroyed the True Dharma that the body falls into the Avīci Hell. One reaps what one sows; how could this come from another?
If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the Tathāgata’s True Wheel of Dharma.
To kill one's father or mother, one may seek the Buddha for repentance; but if one slanders the Buddha or the Patriarchs, where can one repent?
In the sandalwood forest, there are no other trees; dense and profound, it is where the lion dwells. In this tranquil realm and secluded grove, he wanders alone;
wild beasts and winged birds all flee far away.
Candana is a tree of the Western Heaven; here it is translated as "Bestower of Joy. This indicates its place of origin, where there are no thorns at all;
thus, it serves as a metaphor for the single, true realm of the Mahāyāna, which is pure and without admixture. The lion is a metaphor for the King of Dharma.
Indeed, this realm is the dwelling place of the Great Dharma King alone, and the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) cannot reside therein.
Therefore it is said: "The running beasts and flying birds all flee far away.
When the lion cub is followed by the crowd, at three years of age he is already able to let out a great roar. If a jackal should pursue the Dharma King,"
A hundred-year-old monster opens its mouth in vain.

A lion’s cub, having been born for only three years, is already able to roar; yet when a jackal or other wild beast attempts to imitate it, even after a thousand or ten thousand years, it produces only the sound of a monster.
So too is it with those of the Lesser Vehicle who accumulate practices and merit: though they may do so for a long time...
Even after passing through thousands of millions of kalpas, one would ultimately be unable to reach the stage of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Yet when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he declared, "In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored. Furthermore, how could Master Yongjia have required the accumulation of practice over long kalpas to spend but a single night at Caoxi?
This serves as a metaphor for those of the Mahāyāna: if one gives rise to the true mind in a single thought-moment and returns to the source, one enters directly.
The stage of the Tathāgata is that which those of the Lesser Vehicle accumulate through practice.
Regarding the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, do not harbor human sentiments; if there is doubt that cannot be resolved, one must contend with it directly.
When it comes to practicing benevolence, do not yield; if there is doubt, one must debate it.
"It is not that this mountain monk seeks to assert self and other; rather, I fear that those who practice may fall into the pit of annihilationism or eternalism.
The Master did not delight in disputation; he valued the realization of one who has departed from false views and does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence.
It is neither non-being nor being; it is neither affirmation nor negation. To err by a hair’s breadth is to lose a thousand li. If it is affirmed, the Dragon Girl immediately attains Buddhahood;
if it is denied, the virtuous Seng-xing falls into ruin.
Worldly people know only that right and wrong have no fixed master; they do not realize, however, that there truly is what is truly right and what is truly wrong.
Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* records that Zhijizhang asked Mañjuśrī: "Virtuous One, when you went to the Dragon Palace to preach the Dharma, how many people did you transform?"
Mañjuśrī said, "There is a daughter of the Dragon King Sāgara who is eight years old. She possesses sharp faculties and wisdom capable of reaching the stage of a Bodhisattva.
Suddenly, the entire assembly saw this girl transform into a man, fully endowed with the practices of a Bodhisattva.
He immediately departed for a world in the southern direction, where he sat upon a precious lotus flower and attained perfect enlightenment. — *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*
It is said: "King Virūḍhaka and the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra—Virūḍhaka for slaughtering the Gautama clan, and Sunakṣatra for falsely asserting that all dharmas are empty;
both fell alive into the Avīci Hell. Thus, the retribution for sin and merit is seen instantly, and right and wrong are made manifest.
How can one treat Buddha-nature with such superficiality, or regard True Suchness with such reckless indifference?"
Since my early years, I have accumulated learning; I have also investigated commentaries and sought out the sutras and śāstras.

At first, you studied the Tiantai scriptures, distinguishing names and characteristics without knowing when to stop. You entered the sea to count its sands, only to weary yourself in vain; thus, you were bitterly rebuked by the Tathāgata.
Reproach! What benefit is there in enumerating the treasures of others?
Failing to understand one's own fundamental mind, one merely exerts oneself in vain through discrimination, becoming mired within words and letters.
From the beginning, one has stumbled along, realizing one’s journey was empty; for many years, one has needlessly been a traveler in the dust and wind.
Turning one's back on awakening and aligning with the sensory dust, one must lament for oneself.

One’s spiritual lineage is perverse; one’s understanding is erroneous. Failing to comprehend the Tathāgata’s perfect and sudden teaching, one disregards true emptiness and gives rise to conceptual interpretations based on emotional attachments.
The practitioners of the Two Vehicles possess diligence but lack the bodhicitta; the non-Buddhists possess cleverness but lack true wisdom.
Although the followers of the Two Vehicles practice with great diligence, they lack the conduct of saving others; the non-Buddhists are the most clever, yet they instead cling to the view of self.
They are likewise ignorant and deluded, as petty as children. From an empty fist, they give rise to the notion of a real object;
these ordinary people, lacking knowledge, mistakenly take skillful means for the ultimate.
Clinging to the finger as the moon, they labor in vain, falsely fabricating strange illusions within the phenomena of the sense faculties and their objects.
The teachings of the sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon. Once the moon has been seen, one understands that what was pointed to is ultimately not the moon itself.
If one were to further grasp the finger and mistake it for the essence of the moon, would this not be a lack of wisdom?
When not seeing even a single dharma, one is then called a Tathāgata; only then can one be named Avalokiteśvara.
Ordinary beings grasp at appearances as being existent; Śrāvakas speak of ultimate emptiness; Bodhisattvas realize that the very substance of things is itself empty.
If one sees something seen, one is an ordinary being; if one sees nothing seen, one is still halfway there. If one perceives objects...
At that time, there is nothing seen; even the seeing of "nothing seen" is absent, yet there is no [subjective] seeing.

Without abandoning all phenomena and without being identical to all phenomena—this is the abiding of dharmas in their own dharma-position, wherein the characteristics of the world are eternally constant—only then does one attain mastery.
When one has realized this, the nature of karma is fundamentally empty; when one has not yet realized it, one must still repay past debts.
When there is nothing seen upon realization, both sin and merit are fundamentally empty; when one has not yet attained the emptiness of nature, cause and effect remain distinct and clear.
Starving, one encounters a royal feast yet cannot eat; sick, one meets the King of Physicians, yet how can one be cured?
The Master exhorts students: having fortunately encountered the True Lineage in this life, you must penetrate it directly.

Whether advancing or retreating, whether with faith or without faith, it is like being hungry and waiting for food, yet when the King bestows a banquet, you do not eat; or like seeking a physician while suffering from illness, yet the physician...
The King offered him medicine, but he would not accept it; thus, how could his hunger be satiated, and how could his illness be restored?
Through the power of wisdom and insight cultivated while dwelling in desire, one may produce a lotus amidst fire that never perishes.
Not seeing that which is desirable, the mind remains undisturbed; this is the capacity of the Hinayana practitioner.
Seeing that which is desirable yet the mind remains undisturbed—this is a person of immeasurable greatness, like a lotus growing from within fire.
Vīradatta committed a grave offense yet awakened to the non-arising of phenomena; he attained Buddhahood long ago and remains present even now.
This Bhikṣu Vīradatta was originally a handsome man, and thus his monastic appearance was exceptionally distinguished.

While begging for alms, he arrived at the house of an elder; the daughter saw him and became enamored of him. Her longing did not cease, and she fell ill until she was on the verge of death. Her mother, out of deep affection, suffered greatly.
He then devised a plan to entice the bhikṣu, saying, "My daughter wishes to hear the Dharma; my teacher should visit her frequently to instruct her.
He made this request two or three times until the bhikṣu, having no other choice, complied with his command. Consequently, time passed by in a slow and lingering manner.
Although the girl’s illness had subsided, her husband discovered it and intended to kill his wife. When the bhikṣu heard of this, he did not dare go there, and the girl became terrified.

The husband was killed. Furthermore, she harbored thoughts toward a bhikṣu and consequently administered poison to her husband. When the husband died, the bhikṣu heard of it and felt great remorse, saying:
"That this lustful murder occurred was entirely due to me. If I die and fall into the Avīci hell like an arrow, I shall not dare to wear even these three robes;
I shall hang them upon my mendicant’s staff. Raising his voice, he cried out: "I have committed a root offense!"
"Sin! Who will confess this sin for me? He went to a vihāra and encountered the Venerable Niṅjùduōluó (Nigrodha). The Venerable admonished him, saying: "Investigate the nature of sin;
it is ultimately unobtainable. He then spoke a verse: "All phenomena are like reflections in a mirror, And also like the moon in the water.
The deluded minds of ordinary people Distinguish between ignorance, anger, and craving. The bhikṣu attained sudden and great enlightenment. As he responded...
At that time, he who was endowed with the ten titles went to a world in the western direction and attained equal and perfect enlightenment, being named the Tathāgata Ratnacandra.
Having realized non-arising, he knew there is no cessation; therefore, it is said that he exists even now.
The Lion’s Roar. Fearlessly proclaimed. Deeply lamenting the deluded and stubborn *ḍa*.
Regarding phonology: "I am the Dharma King; I possess mastery over the Dharma. Like the lion's roar, he is entirely fearless.

The Lesser Vehicle is lamentable, for they are exclusively attached to the observance and violation of precepts, thereby binding themselves. "Deluded" (*bongdong*) means dark and dull-witted. "*Ḍa*" refers to...
The "ox-neck" refers to the extremely coarse skin on the upper part of the neck.
One knows only that committing a grave offense obstructs bodhi, yet fails to see the Tathāgata’s secret instruction.
The head [of this section] follows below in the text.
There were two bhikṣus who committed the offenses of lust and killing; Upāli and Śrīgupta increased their karmic fetters through their transgressions.
The Great Being Vimalakīrti suddenly dispelled their doubts, just as the blazing sun melts away frost and snow.
There were two bhikṣus who had built a hut in the mountains to practice their cultivation. Once, one bhikṣu went out while the other was sleeping soundly within the hut.
A wood-gathering woman took advantage of his sleep and committed adultery with him. When the bhikṣu awoke, he was displeased and let out a loud cry.
His companion from the same hut happened to arrive and pursued the woman swiftly; she fell over a cliff and died. The two bhikṣus...
He said: "One has committed sexual misconduct and one has committed killing; although each acted unintentionally, the disciples of the Buddha feel ashamed and do not dare to question the Buddha.
They have therefore gone to Upāli to seek absolution. Upāli, who was a strict observer of the precepts, assigned a formal offense (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) to both of them.
Just then, Vimalakīrti arrived and said to him: "Do not further increase the offenses of these two bhikṣus. You should simply eliminate them; do not disturb their minds."
Why is this so? That nature of sin does not exist within, nor does it exist without, nor does it exist in between.
As the Buddha has taught, one should know that the Hīnayāna is like the glow of a firefly, while the Mahāyāna is like the blazing sun.
The nature of sin is fundamentally empty, just like the morning frost and spring snow.
The power of inconceivable liberation is as boundless as the sands of the Ganges.
This power of liberation cannot be fathomed by intellect, nor can it be grasped by ordinary consciousness. When its great function manifests before one, it is all-pervasive.
Exhausting kalpas, it can never be fully repaid.
One would dare not decline the labor of providing the four types of offerings; even ten thousand measures of gold could be spent upon it.
The jewel of the mind is priceless for its benefit to both self and others; though worldly treasures be many, they cannot recompense such profound generosity.
Even grinding one's bones to dust would not suffice as recompense. A single phrase, clearly realized, transcends ten billion worlds.
Its grace is vast and difficult to repay;
it is the King of Dharmas, most supreme and victorious, testified to by all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "All Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate;
all Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter through perfect penetration; those who practice and study in the future should rely upon this very method."
I now explain this wish-fulfilling jewel. Those who believe and accept it will all be in accord with it;

every person shall be fully endowed with it, and each shall achieve perfect realization. It is only because they have been away from home for so long that they do not dare to believe and accept it—just like a destitute son who turns his back on his father and fails to recognize his family’s treasures.
Seeing clearly, there is not a single thing; there is neither person nor Buddha.
When the sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted, both object and self vanish.
The great trichiliocosm is but a bubble on the sea; all sages and worthies are like a flash of lightning.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When one person gives rise to true awakening and returns to the source, this emptiness of the ten directions completely vanishes;
how much more so the various dharma-realms within that emptiness? It further states: "Emptiness arises within Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean."
The world is unreal; how could the noble sages be anything but real? Like a flash of lightning or a floating bubble, all are but illusory appearances.
Even if an iron wheel were to spin upon the crown of one’s head, one’s perfect clarity of concentration and wisdom shall never be lost.
It is simply because one has sufficient faith and maintains mastery that the sun might become cold and the moon might become hot, yet the various māras cannot destroy this true teaching.
That which is real is difficult to extinguish; that which is false is easy to remove.
"The majestic elephant carriage advances in vain upon the road; who has seen a mantis able to block its tracks?
This concludes the meaning of the preceding lines, stating that the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva dwelling in the world is like the carriage of a great elephant.

As they advance upon the great path, those various māras desire to create obstacles and cause ruin; yet they are like a cicada bristling its forelegs to block the ruts of a chariot—it is merely seeking its own destruction.
A great elephant does not traverse the narrow paths of rabbits; one of great awakening is not constrained by minor details.
A superior practitioner of the Mahāyāna possesses mastery over all phenomena; how could they be preoccupied with considerations of time or place?
Furthermore, the fruits realized by those of the Hīnayāna are exactly like rabbit paths—they are not grounds upon which the great elephant wanders.
Do not slander the vast expanse with your limited perspective. I have not yet finished; I shall now resolve this for you.
"The vast expanse" refers to the true color of Heaven. Are you grasping a pen to peer into that Heaven?

This Way cannot be known through discursive thought, nor can it be realized through intellectual calculation. How could those of small roots and small capacity possibly fathom the Great [Wisdom] of the Tathāgata?
The realm of Perfect Enlightenment can never be such [a limited thing]. It is like peering at the sky through a tube:
it is the vessel that is small, not that the sky is partial. How could one say the sky is small? What I have now resolved is merely for the sake of sentient beings who have not yet understood.
Nevertheless, even so, Yongjia cannot help but be overly earnest and doting; had he encountered Lingyan...
Postscript to Master Baoguo’s Commentary on the Song of Realizing the Way (Concluded).
When I first tied my hair in a topknot and followed a teacher, I used the *Analects* and *Mencius* to dispel my ignorance.

In seeking their commentaries and exegeses, I invariably took Chen Yongzhi as my authority for the *Analects* and Xu Yuncheng as my authority for the *Mencius*. Although these two scholars possessed literary elegance, their reasoning was occasionally obscure.

Upon examining the commentaries of Wang Anshi (Shu Wang), however, I found that his words were concise yet his principles were complete. Thus I realized that Chen and Xu intended for people to know [the texts], whereas Shu...
O King, one desires that people reflect. The teachers of antiquity feared only that people would not reflect; the teachers of today fear only that people will not know.
Previously, I observed the various commentaries on the *Song of Realizing the Way*, all of which were similar to those of Chen and Xu.
However, upon observing the commentary by the Venerable Master Narayan (Nenghai), it was exactly like that of Wang Anshi and differed from Chen and Xu. This song is...

This was recorded by Chan Master Zhengjue of Yongjia. Zhengjue had originally practiced *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. One day, upon opening the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment.
He then went to see the Sixth Patriarch; he circumambulated the meditation seat three times and stood there shaking his monk’s staff. The Patriarch rebuked him, saying:
"Now, a bhikṣu is endowed with three thousand dignified demeanors and eighty thousand subtle practices. From what direction have you come, Venerable Sir?"

He gave rise to great conceit. The Master said, "The matter of birth and death is great; impermanence is swift. The Patriarch asked, "Why do you not realize non-arising? Why do you fail to understand that there is no swiftness?
The Master said, "Realizing it is non-arising, I understand that fundamentally there is no swiftness.

The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. After a short while, the Master took his leave to return home. The Patriarch said, "Is your return too soon? The Master said, "Since it is fundamentally neither movement nor stillness, how could there be [a departure]?"
“Swift! the Patriarch said. “Who knows that this is neither movement nor stillness? The Master said, “It is you, O Benevolent One, who give rise to discrimination.

The Patriarch said, “You have attained the state of non-arising quite well. The Master said, “If there is no arising, how can there be intention? The Patriarch said, “If it is not intention, then who gives rise to discrimination?
The Master said, “Even discrimination is not intention. The Patriarch said, “Excellent, excellent! To bring this up is the realization of True Awakening.”
The composition [of this work] can thus be understood. He then stayed for one night and composed this song to certify his realization of the Way; it spread widely throughout the world.

Later, an Indian monk brought it back to the Western Heaven (India), where it was called the *Sūtra of Certification of the Way*. Everyone received and upheld it, just as those in China uphold the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
In my later years, I settled my mind upon this Way with great earnestness. It happened that his disciple, Huìrán of Zuì, [came to me].
I paid him a visit and he presented me with this text. I read it three times, and before I knew it, my mind was suddenly liberated like water dissolving;
my spirit soared as I grasped its essential meaning. Although more than a hundred years have passed since the time of Yongjia, it was as if we were conversing at the same table.

Could this not be because the Venerable Master Lingyan has brought me to this state? It is very much like Linji’s study under Huangbo, where he suffered three blows from the master’s "poisoned hand" before finally [attaining realization].
He understood the meaning of the pain and itching, and upon seeing Dàyú, he realized the old man’s heart was filled with compassion; he then remarked, "The Buddha-dharma is not that much.
He went to Huangbo to consult him again. Huangbo, knowing the reason for his return, said to him: "How could the winds of karma have blown you back to Dàyú?"
"I shall give you a beating with a rotten club. Before he had even finished speaking, Linji struck him with a palm.
"If I were to arrive at Lingyan, I would not fail to emulate Linji’s action. For instance, Lingyan’s face is a thousand fathoms wide and a hundred feet thick."
"Friends, would you dare to strike? If you can discern with absolute clarity, then give him a slap.

On the first day of the month in the *mǎng* period of the *Cǐyǐn* year of the Xiǎngxìng era (1146), the disciple who has studied under him, the Right Officer of the Bureau of Salaries, specially appointed to serve at South Peak in Suzhou, Méi Rǔnéng, respectfully wrote this preface.
